title: MoE long-horizon attention field notes and experiment log
content:
Purpose:
This doc records hands-on profiling and benchmark notes for MoE models when serving very long contexts (up to 65k tokens). Goal is to capture emergent bottlenecks that are architecture-specific (Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen variants) and routing-specific (k-top, soft-gating, capacity factor) so we can add concrete fixes to the runtime: scheduling knobs, prefetching heuristics, and memory layout adjustments.

Context and motivation:
- Customers are starting to push >32k and up to 65k effective contexts for retrieval-augmented generation and multimodal transcripts.
- MoE sharded experts + KV cache scaling changes runtime behavior compared to dense models: routing adds irregular per-token work, expert hot spots, and more frequent memory allocation churn.
- We need practical mitigations to maintain p50/p95 latency SLOs while preserving throughput and model quality.

Testbed summary:
- Hardware: 4x A100 80GB (NVLink enabled) per pod, Docker runtime with CUDA 12.3, NCCL 2.18.
- Models tested: llama-70b-moep (16 experts), mistral-22b-moep (8 experts), qwen-14b-moep (12 experts). Variants include fp16 and 4-bit group-wise quant (gptq-like).
- Sequence lengths: 2k, 16k, 32k, 65k. Batch sizes: 1, 4, 16 depending on sequence length.
- Routing configs: topk=2/4, capacity_factor=1.0/1.5/2.0, soft_router temperature sweep 0.1->1.0.
- Measurement tools: nvprof/ncu lightweight, CUPTI kernel timelines, python tracers (pyinstrument), our internal token-level latency tracer (trace-id per request).

High-level observations (summary):
1) KV-cache IO and scatter/gather overhead dominates beyond ~16k tokens. For all MoE models, time per token increases sublinearly at first, then sharply after a threshold as the cache grows and KV lookups cross internal tiling boundaries.
2) Routing latency variance is model-dependent: Mistral variant exhibits larger per-token variance due to its narrower per-token compute and higher router frequency (router called at more layers). Llama's wider layers amortize routing cost better.
3) Expert hot spots cause local GPU memory pressure and kernel switching overhead on A100; when capacity_factor>1.5 and topk=4 the runtime hits more frequent kernel resubmissions and small kernels that underutilize SMs.
4) Quantized models reduce token wall time for dense layers but routing and KV IO remain dominant; 4-bit helps but only when expert selection is stable.

Detailed traces and examples:
- Example p95 breakdown for llama-70b-moep at 32k tokens, batch=1, topk=2, capacity=1.5 (fp16):
  - total generation time per token (avg): 280ms
  - attention kernel compute: 90ms
  - routing overhead (gating + scatter): 45ms
  - KV-cache read/merge: 70ms
  - memory allocations/GC: 30ms
  - kernel dispatch + small-kernel overhead: 25ms
  - other (IO, scheduling): 20ms
Notes: KV-cache here includes copy+reorder for concatenated long context. The 30ms memory allocation time is mostly from temporary buffers used by the router when topk is >2.

Hypotheses and experiments run (log):
1) Prefetch window sizing for KV cache
   - Hypothesis: Increasing prefetch window reduces runtime stalls by overlapping KV IO with compute; with long contexts we should prefetch earlier but only for likely-to-be-used prefixes.
   - Experiment: prefetch distance = {1, 4, 8, 16} tokens ahead; prefetch only for experts selected by gating prob >0.2.
   - Result: distance=8 gave best p95 improvement (~11% lower). distance>=16 increased memory tail and caused OOMs for batch>1.

2) Routing aggregation micro-batching
   - Hypothesis: Aggregate routing decisions across a micro-batch of tokens (windowed micro-batching) to amortize small kernels and reduce kernel launch overhead.
   - Implementation note: add token-window grouping inside Router operator, maintain ordering with token-offsets.
   - Result: For topk=4, micro-batch=8 tokens reduced kernel dispatch overhead by 38% but increased peak GPU memory by 6%. p95 improved but p50 unchanged.

3) KV layout change: shard-aligned layout vs contiguous per-layer layout
   - Hypothesis: Aligning KV shards to expert assignment reduces scatter costs when composing output for topk>1.
   - Result: Shard-aligned layout reduced KV merge time by ~22% on Llama and ~18% on Qwen. Implementation complexity moderate; requires changes to checkpoint loader and on-disk format.

4) Adaptive capacity_factor per-token
   - Hypothesis: Lower capacity for tokens with low gating entropy saves compute and avoids moving large numbers of tokens to expensive expert kernels.
   - Heuristic used: capacity = base + entropy_normalized * scale
   - Result: Reduced average token work by ~9% and decreased p95 variance. Quality impact (ROUGE) on test prompts: negligible within noise (0.2 points).

Architecture-specific notes:
- Llama (70b moep):
  - Tends to have fewer routed layers; routing concentrated reduces scatter frequency. The attention kernels are larger and more efficient on A100, so KV and routing overhead fraction is relatively higher. Benefit from shard-aligned KV layout was largest here.
  - Mistral-style MoE (22b):
  - Router invoked at more layers; smaller dense kernels mean more frequent small-kernel overhead. Prefetch helped less because compute windows are smaller and overlap is harder to expose. Micro-batching routing provided the most benefit here.
  - Qwen (14b moep):
  - Middle ground: fewer router layers than Mistral, but experts are more memory-heavy. Memory churn and allocations showed up as the main p95 culprit. Reducing temporary buffer allocation and reusing pre-allocated pools improved stability.

Operational mitigations we prototyped:
- Pre-allocated per-request temporary buffer pool (locked to request lifetime). Cuts allocation overhead and GC spikes. Implemented as an arena allocator inside runtime.
- Router micro-batching with bounded lookahead: window size default=8 tokens, max window=16. Work-steering to avoid large memory spikes per batch.
- KV shard on-disk layout option (flag guarded): toggle to load KV in shard-aligned memory; requires model-conversion tool (we prototyped a converter).
- Entropy-driven adaptive capacity factor: default base=1.0, scale=1.0, clamp [0.7, 2.0].

Smoke commands and profiler snippets used (repro):
- python perf_runner.py --model llama-70b-moep --seq-len 32768 --batch 1 --topk 2 --cap 1.5 --quant fp16 --trace-token-level --out traces/llama-32k-top2.json
- ncu --set full --target-processes=all --export csv -o ncu_llama_32k traces/llama-32k.top2
- internal trace collector: cat traces/llama-32k-top2.json | jq '.tokens | map(.latency_ms) | add / length'

Open action items (next steps):
- INF-1243: Bake router micro-batching into a feature-flagged runtime operator (owner: Mate0 Ruiz). Priority: P1 for 32k+ contexts.
- GH-PR: runtime#1102 add arena allocator + reuse pools (owner: Jingwen). Blocker: confirm no regressions on non-MoE dense models.
- Model conversion: create a lightweight converter to produce shard-aligned KV files for customers willing to trade on-disk compatibility for perf gains (owner: Ravi).
- Rollout plan: Canary on dedicated nodes only; monitor p50/p95 and memory OOMs for first 48h.

Unresolved questions and notes to investigate later:
- Does topk variance correlate with token semantics (i.e., are certain tokens consistently heavy)? We have anecdotal evidence but need a corpus-wide gating entropy analysis.
- How much of the p95 is from PCIe/NVLink cross-device copy at 65k contexts when requests touch many experts on different GPUs? Need process-level NVLink tracing.
- Investigate NCCL rendezvous costs when routing causes dynamic all-to-all across experts. Could we use scheduled rendezvous windows to amortize?

Appendix: quick findings table (single-line bullets):
- Prefetch distance=8 preferred, >=16 causes OOMs for batch>1.
- Micro-batching routing reduces kernel-launch overhead but increases memory by ~5-8%.
- Shard-aligned KV layout gives ~20% KV merge improvement on average.
- Adaptive capacity factor reduces avg token compute ~9% with minimal quality regression.
- Quantization helps dense kernels but routing remains the bottleneck; focus on routing/IO first for long-context MoE.

Notes to reviewers: this is a field log, contains rough numbers and heuristics. If we pursue any of these mitigations, we should add deterministic microbenchmarks and a reproducible dataset of long-context prompts (both synthetic and real transcripts).

End of notes.
